source_document.body:
Nearly all food and drink businesses surveyed identified serious labor rights violations in their supply chains during the past year, according to research commissioned by the British Standards Institution (BSI) and the Chartered Institute of Procurement & Supply (CIPS). At 97%, food and beverage respondents reported the highest rate of any industry surveyed.
What’s Related
The findings also point to weaknesses in how businesses track their response. Only 36% of food and drink firms could demonstrate the impact of whistleblowing and other channels for reporting concerns, the lowest among the industries studied.
Meanwhile, 39% did not require suppliers to identify their own suppliers in contracts. That leaves companies with less information about the businesses and workers involved further down their supply chains.
Together, the findings show that identifying labor problems and demonstrating improvements for workers remain separate challenges. The 97% figure covers several types of violations and should not be read as a finding that every affected company discovered forced labor.
RELATED: $2.03 an Hour: Labor Dept. Finds Major Wage Violations at Warehouse
Too many unanswered questions
The research found a gap between what business leaders believe they can prove and how much of their supply chains they can actually see. Across industries, 80% said they had enough evidence to demonstrate that their supply chains were free from violations, while only 22% reported comprehensive visibility of third-party suppliers.
For food and drink companies, the lack of supplier disclosure requirements adds another obstacle. Knowing a direct supplier does not necessarily mean knowing which businesses provide its ingredients, materials, or services, or what conditions workers face at those businesses.
“The challenge is then being able to demonstrate impact and show that these interventions are improving outcomes for workers. Addressing modern slavery risk is about driving meaningful change,” said Harold Pradal, president of assurance services at BSI.
What happens after a violation is found?
The research also examined how companies respond when they uncover problems. BSI’s U.S. announcement said 53% worked with suppliers to address violations rather than immediately ending contracts, while 11% described their response as limited.
However, continuing a supplier relationship does not, by itself, show that working conditions have improved. The food and beverage findings raise a similar question about reporting channels: businesses may have ways for workers to raise concerns without being able to show what changed afterward.
“The challenge is no longer whether businesses are taking action, but whether they can demonstrate that their action is driving real improvements for vulnerable workers,” Pradal said.
